alt: Story quiz: a Nobel Prize came out of a 4th-century recipe. What detail did everyone miss?
Story answer: cold water. Full story at 12:00.

caption:
A Nobel Prize was hiding in a 1,600-year-old first-aid book.

Ge Hong's 4th-century handbook said: for fevers, soak a handful of sweet wormwood in water, wring out the juice, drink it. In the 1970s Tu Youyou's team kept failing to get a working malaria extract. She noticed the recipe never said boil. Heat was destroying the compound. Cold extraction worked: artemisinin, now a frontline malaria drug. Nobel Prize, 2015.

Tag the friend who never reads the instructions. Tu Youyou read them twice. 😅

Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic. Modern artemisinin is purified and dosed; wormwood juice is not a treatment.

Instructions or vibes?

caption:
A student told Confucius he'd mastered kindness.

Tsze-kung: "What I do not wish men to do to me, I also wish not to do to men." Confucius: "Ts'ze, you have not attained to that." (Analects V.11, tr. James Legge)

It sounds like a put-down. It's the opposite. He didn't say the idea was wrong. He said living it is harder than saying it, which means there's still somewhere to get to.

Tag the friend who says "I'm basically a saint." 😇

Story quiz: a 12th-century Seville doctor tested a new throat surgery on someone first. Who?
Story answer: a goat. Full story at 12:00.

caption:
Medieval Seville's best doctor tested surgery on a goat first.

Ibn Zuhr (Avenzoar) performed a tracheotomy on a goat to show it could be done safely before anyone tried it on a person. In Córdoba, al-Zahrawi wrote a thirty-volume medical encyclopedia and drew the tools he used. In Málaga, Ibn al-Baytar listed about 1,400 simple medicines. Test it, draw it, write it down: al-Andalus, a thousand years ago.

Tag the friend who'd volunteer the goat. 🐐

Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.

Goat or you?

#history #medicalhistory #alandalus #science #curiosity

caption:
The friend who always pays might be the happiest one at the table.

Across 136 countries, people who'd spent money on others in the past month reported more wellbeing in 120 of them (Aknin et al., 2013). Linked, not proven to cause it. A small 2008 experiment (46 people, Science) found spending on someone else beat spending on yourself; later studies found smaller effects. So: promising, not magic.

Cheap experiment: £3, one coffee, one person, don't post it.

Tag the friend who always pays. It's your round. ☕

Whose round?

caption:
Bad mood? An emperor's fix: think about other people.

Not their faults. Their best bits. Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.48 (Long): "When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee; for instance, the activity of one, and the modesty of another, and the liberality of a third."

Pick four people. One good quality each. Tell one of them.

caption:
A medical book in Timbuktu names a tree nobody can find.

Timbuktu scholars wrote handbooks of diagnoses and cures from plants, animals and minerals, alongside prayers. Many entries name local trees in Bambara and other languages, and some, like a tree called Ṣukuru, scholars still can't identify. A 2011 survey counted more than 100,000 manuscripts in at least 408 private family libraries in Mali.

Tag the friend who'd go looking for it. 🌳

Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.

caption:
An emperor of Rome wrote this note to himself, which means even Marcus Aurelius stood in a doorway once waiting for a thank you that never came.

His point: you did the good thing, they got the good thing. Looking for a third thing (credit, a favour back) is where the annoyance comes from. The kindness was already finished.

caption:
Everyone has the friend who grabs the bill before you've found your wallet. Turns out they might be getting something out of it.

One small brain-scan study (19 people, Science 2007) found that giving to charity lit up reward areas, even when the gift was compulsory, and more when it was chosen. A Gallup-based study across 136 countries linked spending on others to more wellbeing in 120 of them. Linked, not proven to cause it.
